#3001. You can turn Claude artifacts into Windows and Mac apps now – here’s how

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Anthropic's new 'install as app' feature makes it easy to turn your Claude artifacts into desktop apps on your computer - with some limitations.

Anthropic is making its Claude artifacts available as desktop apps, meaning you can share and more easily access your most-repeated tasks on your computer. The “install as app” feature is available in beta for all free and paid Claude plans and works on both Mac and Windows, but not Linux.

Also: 4 ways Anthropic’s Claude Sheets beat using a Google Sheets connector

Anthropic first released artifacts in 2024. Since then, they’ve become a way to standardize and repeat tasks users do regularly, especially at work. Previously, artifacts ran via your Claude window or in a browser. By splicing them out as distinct desktop apps, you can now run different Claude queries while also using your artifacts locally, or use those apps without opening Claude at all.

“When an artifact is installed as a Mac or Windows app, it gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude. You can share it with others, and it needs your permission before it can interact with your computer,” Anthropic said.

Artifact apps can still access Claude and any connectors you’re using, and they update automatically when you edit the artifact itself in Claude. When apps request something from Claude, though, that goes toward your Claude usage limits, which are lowest for free users.

Anthropic said the app feature is meant to streamline building apps for both developer and non-developer work.

Also: Can AI plan terrorist attacks? US tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok

The update clarifies where AI software for work is headed. Claude is already more of an AI-powered work suite than a single helpful chatbot for many organizations. Evidently, people are using tools like artifacts frequently enough — and simultaneously with other Claude features — that they need those Claude-based tools to function like discrete bits of software on their own.

“If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention,” Anthropic said.

Claude artifact apps don’t have the same functionality as apps you could build using Claude Code, though. Even if you don’t need Claude open for these apps to work, you’ll still need to be signed in to Claude and have internet access, so they’re not an entirely portable or off-grid option.

The feature’s support page also notes that legacy artifacts, “live artifacts from Claude Cowork,” and artifacts generated from templates like Docs, Slides, and Sheets can’t be installed as desktop apps.

First, make sure Claude for Mac or Windows is updated. You can try the “install as app” feature, which is in beta for all free and paid plans, via Claude’s Share menu. Select the Install as app option, which will then download the artifact you chose to your desktop. From there, set permissions as needed.

Permissions range from the default (whatever they are in a browser) to app-specific permissions like sending notifications and full computer access.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a local AI stack that’s completely free

Full computer access means the artifact app can “run programs and read, change, or delete your files without asking each time,” Anthropic said, so proceed carefully. Every time you edit and update the artifact (and thus the app), Claude will ask you to confirm permissions again, so you’ll ideally have regular checkpoints to revise access. Still, there are some guardrails in place: Anthropic only lets you give full computer access to apps you’ve made yourself. For Team and Enterprise plans, that extends to any apps made by your coworkers.

“Anthropic doesn’t review apps before you install them, so only give full access to apps you trust,” the company said.

For Claude Enterprise plans, the install-as-app feature is off entirely until an admin turns it on in Organization settings.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates are down this morning, but could seesaw back up tomorrow.

Another day, another substantial swing. This one's lower, but don't count on it starting a trend: We keep seeing mortgage rates move back and forth, but no one's expecting rates to take a dive. If you're watching this space because you're waiting to refinance, it's unlikely your wait is about to end.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.13% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 25 basis points lower than yesterday and unchanged from a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

The amount of day-to-day discrepancy we've been seeing prompted me to take a little cruise around the web this morning to see what 30-year rates lenders are advertising. Mortgage lenders' rates are never identical, but when we're seeing rapid change, the gaps between lenders tend to widen — and that's for sure what I saw. I looked at six different lenders, and saw a nearly 70-basis-point difference between the highest and lowest APRs. (And yes, that was looking for the same loan amount, location and so on.)

My point is, whether you're looking to buy or refinance, make sure to shop multiple lenders. You're the same candidate bringing the same financials to each one, but you could end up with extremely different rate quotes. And it pays to compare. Freddie Mac estimates that comparing at least two lenders could save you up to $600 per year in interest. Compare four or more, and that savings is over $1,200 annually.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context. For more, keep reading below the charts.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Mortgage rates may be lower today, but like I mentioned above, it's been more of a seesaw than a ski slope — and we may be about to hit the high side again. The latest Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index is due out tomorrow morning. Recently, when rates have moved higher, inflation's been in the mix.

Strong inflation's generally bad for borrowing, including to buy a home, because higher interest rates are the remedy. Raising the federal funds rate (the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers of the Federal Reserve actually set) is the Fed's main tactic for managing inflation. While the Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, its decisions influence the entire economy. That includes mortgage lenders, who tend to adjust rates ahead of its decisions.

We already know how PCE's likely to go, since it's the last of the three big inflation measures to be released. We've already gotten last month's Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index. October's CPI came in worse than predicted, showing widespread price increases. (When most of the increase is driven by one area, it's easier to be optimistic that inflation can be contained.) And October’s PPI showed wholesale inflation climbed at its fastest pace in almost four years. PPI measures the price businesses pay for things, so it's often a preview of what consumers could face once those costs get passed along.

Predictions for October PCE aren't great, so at this point the hope is that the numbers aren't even worse than expected. And again, PCE's out tomorrow morning. We'll know whether we're getting seconds (actually, thirds) of bad October inflation news well before the turkey hits the table on Thursday.

Markets are currently anticipating a quarter-point hike at the Fed's December meeting. Even though that'll remain the most likely outcome, a poor showing from PCE could spark speculation about a half-point hike. That probably won't be good for mortgage rates.

But back to the upcoming holiday: Markets will be closed on Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, so we'll all have a bit of a break this week. Mortgage rates don't move much when the markets aren't moving. I won't be here to talk to you about mortgage rates, either, 'cause NerdWallet gives us Thursday and Friday off. Happy Thanksgiving!

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you could start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.63% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

» Stay informed: Check out NerdWallet's mortgage news hub for all our latest coverage.

The rate you see advertised is a sample rate — usually for a borrower with perfect credit, making a big down payment, and paying for mortgage points. That won't match every buyer's circumstances.

In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your:

Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles.

#2996. The FCC Approved a Million SpaceX Satellites for Data Centers in Space

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

"I think this is a mistake," one astrophysicist tells CNET.

The Federal Communications Commission has approved SpaceX’s request to launch 1 million AI-equipped satellites to create vast data centers in space.

SpaceX initially filed an application in May asking for permission to launch the satellites, collectively known as Starmind. The FCC’s approval requires that SpaceX launch its first data center satellite by 2030 and meet the 1 million mark by 2040.

“It’s just really abrogating their responsibility to go, ‘Well, this is a project they’re proposing. Is this actually safe?’” Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist who tracks satellite launches, told CNET. “It’s a blank check. Launch as many satellites as you can, and we’ll just see what happens. I think this is a mistake on the FCC’s part.”

Orbital data centers have long been a goal of SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, becoming a pivotal part of his pitch to investors ahead of the company’s IPO in June.

“You’re power-constrained on Earth. Space has the advantage that it’s always sunny,” Musk said in March.

On its web page for Starmind, SpaceX touts its high-efficiency solar arrays on the planned satellites and the cooling benefits of space. It says that high-speed laser links will beam the AI results back to Earth through Starlink’s constellation.

Space experts I’ve talked to this year about Starmind have been skeptical. The technical challenges alone are dizzying; the scale of SpaceX’s ambitions is hard to swallow.

It’s taken seven years for Starlink to grow its constellation to 11,195 satellites, and that was already an unprecedented feat. Is it possible to get to 1 million satellites in 14 years?

“We do not have the launch capacity for any of this,” Ian Christensen, senior director at the Secure World Foundation, told me in a previous interview. “Not even within SpaceX to do their own constellation, let alone the other constellations planned.”

SpaceX has increasingly prioritized launching its own satellites instead of letting commercial customers hitch a ride on their rockets. Starlink’s share of SpaceX missions has gone from 54% of its Falcon 9 rocket’s missions in 2020 to about 79% in 2026, according to a Reuters analysis. One analysis estimates that SpaceX would have to launch 5,000 Starship rockets a year to meet its goal — a staggering increase from 330 rockets that launched last year in total.

Scientists have already been ringing alarm bells about overcrowded orbits as they exist now. The more satellites in space, the more difficult it is for operators to maneuver around each other. A single crash could turn into decades of orbital debris, which could cause a chain reaction that eventually makes space inoperable for everyone. And burning up all those satellites in the atmosphere when they reach the end of their lives has already started to leave ozone-depleting aluminum particles behind. A paper published this week in Earth and Space Chemistry estimated that SpaceX’s data center plan would multiply pollutants in the upper atmosphere by more than 150 times compared to last year.

“There are scientific papers out there raising issues,” McDowell said. “Yes, they’re unproven, but if I say, ‘Yeah, we’re not sure if this is going to destroy the atmosphere and kill us all, but it might,’ is the right reaction to go, ‘Well, you haven’t proven it, so we’re just going to ignore it’?”

The FCC’s approval came despite objections from Amazon, the environmental nonprofit Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility and the American Astronomical Society.

A representative for SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

#2993. Amazon Is Backing More Than 5 Gigawatts of New Nuclear by 2039. This Reactor Developer Could Cash In.

Amazon's 5-gigawatt nuclear push could give X-energy a powerful tailwind, but is the stock worth investing in right now?

By Courtney Carlsen – Nov 25, 2026 at 1:15PM EST

Hyperscalers face a big question: How do you feed power-hungry data centers while working toward net-zero carbon emissions? Amazon (AMZN -2.98%) is betting nuclear energy can help bridge that gap. The company is backing 5 gigawatts of new nuclear power by 2039, with small modular reactor developer X-energy (XE -5.16%) playing a key role.

With projects in the pipeline, Amazon's partnership gives X-energy a powerful backer and an opportunity to prove its nuclear technology can deliver. Could the artificial intelligence (AI) boom help turn this next-generation nuclear stock into a major growth opportunity?

In 2019, Amazon co-founded The Climate Pledge, which calls on signatories to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040. More recently, Amazon laid out plans to cut the carbon intensity of operations by 65% compared with 2019 levels.

A major component of Amazon's carbon-reduction goals involves nuclear energy, which provides carbon-free, reliable, 24/7 baseload power that data centers desperately need. Nuclear energy complements intermittent renewables, like wind and solar power, and numerous hyperscalers, including Microsoft, Meta Platforms, and Alphabet, are signing agreements for nuclear power.

Amazon launched its $2 billion Climate Pledge Fund in 2020, and it used some of those funds to become an early investor in X-energy in October 2024 during its Series C-1 financing round. Amazon provided much-needed project and development funds, and has been central in helping X-energy with the design, licensing, and build-out of its nuclear fuel facility.

X-energy develops the Xe-100 SMR, a high-temperature, gas-cooled nuclear reactor. The Xe-100 uses small graphite pebbles packed with uranium particles and coated in a high-temperature ceramic, and it uses helium gas for cooling. The reactor uses its core physics and heat-resistant fuel to naturally shut down the nuclear reaction and passively dissipate heat without pumps or human intervention.

SMRs are appealing because they are manufactured in modular factory units and can be linked together. For example, each Xe-100 produces 80 megawatts (MW) of electricity and can be linked together, like the 12-unit, 960 MW project planned in Indiana.

Amazon has been crucial for X-energy, helping it fund a four-unit project totaling 320 MW with Energy Northwest in central Washington. It has also committed funding to develop the 12-unit project with American Electric Power at the former coal plant in Indiana. Meanwhile, X-energy's project with Dow in Texas has cleared regulatory review for construction and hopes to deliver power by the early 2030s.

SMRs could completely change how we think about and deploy nuclear energy, and X-energy is one of many start-ups in the space. Amazon has helped X-energy clear regulatory hurdles and secure commercial agreements, giving it a massive leg up on competitors that lack similar backing.

X-energy could be a massive winner over the next decade as the nuclear renaissance unfolds. That said, X-energy's story is still being written, and it will be several years before it deploys its first reactors commercially, making the stock best suited for your watch list for now.

#2991. The Future Is Brighter Than You Think: Why Technology Could Make Humanity Better Off

Lindsey Witmer Collins is Founder and CEO of WLCM.AI, an Inc. 5000 company building AI solutions for enterprises, and Scribbly Books.

​I know how that sounds, and I know it makes me seem uninformed or naive, but I’m really just trying to make an important choice thoughtfully. It’s a choice we all get to make: How do I orient myself to the world I’m in and the one I’m building? And, specifically, I’m curious. What if we ran our projections for the future of humanity in the opposite direction than the doom default? In other words, what if the future is awesome?

Our feeds show many flavors of doom: AI is coming for the jobs, the planet is cooking, the kids can’t look up from their phones and somewhere a robot is learning to do backflips. I build software for a living, including the kind people are nervous about, so I’m not saying this from a hammock. I’m looking for evidence.

A good place to understand where we’re going is to see where we’ve been—to understand what we care about, what we’re capable of and what direction, as a species, we trend toward.

If you were born in 1800, there was, globally, roughly a 43% chance you’d die before your fifth birthday. Today, it’s about 4%, and in most of the world it’s lower than that. Nearly 80% of humanity lived in extreme poverty two centuries ago; by 2019 it was under 10%, and since 1990 the count has dropped by something like 130,000 people every single day. In 1820, 1 adult in 10 could read. We’re at 87% now.

None of that happened by accident. It happened because somebody figured out that germs exist, that a cowpox sore could stop smallpox, that nitrogen could be pulled out of thin air and turned into fertilizer. Somebody built the sewer. Somebody built the washing machine—Hans Rosling used to call it the greatest invention of the industrial revolution, and his argument was basically that it gave his mother back enough hours to read to him.

My great-grandmother could walk into my kitchen today—hot water out of a wall, a box that keeps food cold, a cabinet of medicine that works, the whole of recorded human knowledge in the pocket of my jeans—and conclude she had died and gone to heaven. To me it’s just Monday, and I’m a little annoyed about the traffic.

The pace never slowed down; the headlines just moved on to other things. The International Energy Agency called solar the cheapest electricity in history back in 2020, and it has kept getting cheaper. Lithium-ion battery packs ended 2025 averaging $108 per kilowatt-hour, down 93% since 2010, which is the reason the grid, my electric car and the battery in my lawnmower are all getting electrified without a modicum of drama.

In December 2023, the FDA approved the first CRISPR-based therapy, for people with sickle cell disease—a disease we’ve understood at the molecular level for decades and could do very little about until now. Twenty-five African countries now give malaria vaccines as part of routine childhood shots, and they’re more than 39 million doses in. This year, four astronauts flew around the moon for the first time since 1972, and an mRNA flu shot got approved after beating the traditional one by about 27% in a trial of nearly 50,000 people.

And AI—which we love to fret about—is mostly busy doing the routable work: the reading, the sorting, the first draft, the thousand small lookups. That raises the value of everything it can’t reach, and most of what it can’t reach is other people.

I spend most of my time now on an above-ground mining startup focused on the critical minerals and materials sitting in the U.S.’s retiring infrastructure—EV batteries, solar panels, telecom copper wires and so forth. A surprising share of the next decade’s supply is already here, waiting to be recovered, and it’s on the verge of happening.

What if we get all of the benefits of technology, and we still love each other, and hang out, and chat with the person at the checkout?

Picture a backyard cookout in 2075. Grandma is 120 and bringing her famous potato salad, because the cataract fix was an afternoon, her hip came out of a printer and she’s been weightlifting her entire adult life. The power for the whole event—the grill, the speaker, the car that drove her over—cost roughly nothing, because sunlight is free and we finally got good at storing it. The toddler running laps around the table will learn of malaria only in history books. Somebody’s cousin runs a three-person company that would have needed 40 people in 2020. And we’re still watching live sports in the living room.

If the lines on the charts to keep going the way they’ve gone for 200 years, and if we keep showing up with a side dish, we might end up better than fine.

We’re all makers and builders in our own unique ways, and we build what we see in our mind’s eye. If the only future we picture is the grim one, we might start driving off the road.

I’m going to say we’re building a beautiful and abundant future, and that things will keep getting better. You may say I’m choosing my facts selectively, and you would be correct. There are too many facts, so we all get our pick.

#2990. BYD vs. General Motors: Which Carmaker Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

BYD and GM are both leaning on very different engines, and the valuation gap between them may matter more than either company's EV pitch.

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 25, 2026 at 1:23PM EST

The global automotive market is shifting as electric vehicles challenge traditional engines. Investors must decide if high-growth BYD (BYDDF -2.40%) or the established legacy of General Motors (GM +1.99%) offers a better path forward.

BYD focuses on new-energy vehicles, batteries, and rail transit, establishing itself as a leader in the transition away from fossil fuels. General Motors relies on its massive scale and profit-heavy internal combustion engine sales to fund its own electric transformation. Both are competing for dominance in a rapidly changing transportation landscape.

BYD is a prominent player in the global automotive industry, which is a major part of consumer discretionary stocks. The company designs and sells new-energy vehicles while also operating in electronics, batteries, and rail transit systems. Its footprint covers more than 400 cities worldwide, supported by a massive workforce of nearly 869,622 employees.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $120.4 billion. The company reported a net income of approximately $4.7 billion during this time frame. Revenue growth was roughly negative 4.5% compared to the prior twelve-month period, reflecting recent shifts in the global market.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was nearly 0.7x. This ratio compares total debt to shareholder equity to show how a company funds its operations. Its current ratio, which measures the ability to cover short-term debts with short-term assets, was approximately 0.8x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was nearly negative $14.6 billion, representing the cash remaining after the business covers its day-to-day operations and capital equipment.

General Motors designs and builds a wide variety of trucks, crossovers, and cars, supported by more than 10,000 authorized dealerships globally. The company maintains strategic joint ventures for battery production and vehicle sales, particularly in the Chinese market. It also operates a captive finance arm to provide financing options for customers and dealers.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue was about $187 billion. Net income for the period was approximately $4.0 billion. This represented a revenue growth rate of nearly negative 0.3% as the company navigates the transition to new technology.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio reached roughly 2.1x. This metric indicates the relationship between total debt and shareholders' equity. The current ratio was close to 1.2x, representing the company's short-term liquidity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow reached approximately $11.1 billion.

BYD faces significant challenges due to geopolitical trade tensions, as many regions are considering or imposing tariffs on imported vehicles. The company also operates in a crowded Chinese market where price wars can weigh on financial results. Furthermore, its global expansion requires significant capital investment in diverse regulatory environments.

General Motors appears to be the more conservatively priced option, as it carries a lower multiple of both earnings estimates and sales.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

General Motors has had a decent year, widening its market share in the U.S. to more than 17%, to stay the biggest car seller in the country. Also, hybrids like the Chevy Equinox and Blazer and the EV Cadillac Lyriq have been better sellers than expected, calming some fears that GM was falling behind in the trend toward hybrids and EVs.

The company has also been aggressively buying back shares, which supports the share price in the market and makes profitability appear to be improving on the per-share level. GM also shifted its shares to the Nasdaq Stock Market recently to try and get itself listed on the Nasdaq 100 index, which would also be supportive for shares, given that about $1.4 trillion in assets are indexed to the Nasdaq 100. The company is also lauded on Wall Street for handling the various Trump tariff issues that had generated fears the business would be adversely impacted.

That said, top-line growth is slow, with 2027 revenue seen rising $3 billion to $189 billion and net income exceeding $12 billion, up from about $9 billion expected for full year 2026.

Turning to BYD, while the company doesn't have a U.S. presence, it is one of the top automakers in China. The automaker's September vehicle sales increased about 17% compared to the same month in 2025, headlined by a remarkable 154% jump in overseas shipments of passenger vehicles and pickups. It's part of the company's goal of catching Toyota Motor Co. (TM +2.77%) as the world's largest automaker. Overseas sales were about 39% of BYD's sales in the third quarter. Yet it has its domestic challenges, with Q3 China sales declining more than 18% for BYD, due to intense pricing competition and a hurting Chinese consumer.

Still, foreign sales should help BYD push 2027 sales up 16% in its reporting currency of Chinese yuan, to about $145 billion at today's exchange rate.

So which stock to go with? BYD's push into Europe appears to be going very well, but that is counterbalanced by domestic problems. GM is a bargain price at a forward P/E ratio of 5.8x. The Great Recession bailout by the U.S. federal government showed how important GM is to the U.S. economy. The bet here is that GM's leading position in the world's second-largest car market, the U.S., will continue to hold, and management will continue to find ways to improve returns to shareholders.

Grants don’t have to be repaid, but the money can only go toward school-related costs. Here’s how to use grants to pay for school and how to make them go further.

Grants are one of the best ways you can pay for your education. It’s free money you aren’t expected to pay back.

Grants can be used for tuition, course materials and other cost-of-attendance expenses. Some grants, depending on who awards them, require an application or have requirements you must meet before you can get your money.

Here’s how to use a college grant and what it can pay for.

Federal grants come from the federal government.

State grants come from state programs and often can only be used at schools in that state.

Institutional grants come from your college or university, or even your program or major.

Private grants come from nonprofits, community organizations and individual donors.

To receive a federal grant, you must complete the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). Most states require the FAFSA for state grants, and a few require a separate state application. You’ll need to complete the FAFSA for each year you’re enrolled in school. You may need to meet certain eligibility requirements, such as income limits, to get some grants. The FAFSA is how you apply for the Pell Grant, which is a financial need-based grant. The FAFSA also determines eligibility for federal work-study, which is a job program rather than a grant.

Federal aid, including federal grants, typically requires students to meet satisfactory academic progress. This means you have to maintain a minimum grade point average and be on track to finish your degree on time, as determined by your school. Your school also sets how many credits you must take to qualify for grant funding.

Some grants — typically private or institutional grants — require an additional application that asks for transcripts, letters of recommendation and personal essays. Your school’s financial aid office or the grant provider will have details on applying for specific grants.

After you submit the FAFSA, you’ll receive a financial aid award letter from each school you applied to, which outlines how much in federal, state and institutional grants you’ve been offered. You must accept your aid to receive it.

Most grants will be disbursed directly to your college or university. Your school will apply the grant money first to tuition, fees and any other charges it bills, such as housing or a meal plan.

In some cases, you may receive more grant money than your school bills, which is the best-case scenario. If that happens to you, any leftover funds will likely be refunded to you. Refund timelines vary by school, so it may take some time to get your money. You can get your refund faster by setting up direct deposit with your school. You can then use the funds for other costs approved by your grant — some examples are detailed below.

If you have questions about your grant money, contact your college’s financial aid office.

Grants can help cover cost-of-attendance expenses. Generally, you can use grant money to pay for tuition, textbooks, class materials, transportation, housing and food. Depending on your school’s policies, you can use grant money to cover summer classes or study abroad programs, too.

Some grants come with specific terms about how you can spend them. Check your financial aid award letter or, for a private or institutional grant, the school’s or organization’s website to find specifics.

After your grant is applied to your tuition and school expenses, you can options to fill the gaps between what the grant covers and the total cost of your program. Some options include savings, scholarships, work-study, payment plans, federal student loans or, as a last resort, private loans. By using grants to pay for your college education, you may be able to borrow less.

To maximize the grants you’re eligible to receive, enter accurate information on the FAFSA and complete it as soon as you can — some funds are first-come, first-served. Also, don’t limit yourself to federal or state grants — search and apply for as many privately funded grants as you can find.

Your grant money usually goes straight to your college or university to pay your tuition and fees. Anything that is left over may be disbursed to you for other school-related costs.

Yes, but it depends on your grant. Housing is part of your cost of attendance, so you can use grant money to pay for off-campus rent.

You don’t have to pay back a grant as long as you continue to meet all requirements for the grant, such as staying enrolled. You can use grant money on school and school-related expenses. Some grants may require you to meet eligibility requirements such as a minimum GPA or state residency. If you receive more grant money than your cost of attendance for a given school term, ask your financial aid office if you can put that grant money toward next year’s cost of attendance.

If you have a federal grant like a Pell Grant, these are examples when you may have to repay all or part of the grant:

You received enough scholarship money to reduce your federal aid need.

It depends. You can usually use grant money to buy a laptop. Computers are considered course materials, which fall under cost-of-attendance expenses, so they can be covered by a grant. However, always double-check with the grant provider and your financial aid award letter to ensure that you’re following all restrictions. Whether you can use grant money to cover a laptop depends on your school’s policies and how much grant money you receive.

If you get more grant money than your school bills you, you’ll likely receive the leftover money to spend on other cost-of-attendance expenses. You can use this money on living costs such as transportation or housing. Grant money often goes mostly toward tuition, so a refund isn’t guaranteed.

Grant and scholarship money is generally tax-free when you use it for tuition, required fees, books and required class supplies. If you have additional questions, consider talking to a tax professional.

#2988. The AI Infrastructure Bet That Smart Enterprises Are Making

Paul Deraval, Cofounder & CEO of NinjaCat, is a software veteran with 20+ years driving innovation in martech, AI and agency growth.

Right now, companies of all sizes and sectors are racing to adopt artificial intelligence. Many consider AI the next big thing, and no one wants to miss out.

For many enterprises, this means increasing access to AI tools. They are paying for Claude subscriptions, licensing ChatGPT Enterprise and rolling out Microsoft Copilot across departments. According to Gallup’s latest workplace survey, 47% of employees say their organization integrated AI tools in Q2 2026, up from 41% the previous quarter.

Unfortunately, more tools don’t necessarily equate to better outcomes or higher productivity, and many executives aren’t seeing ROI even as they spend millions on software seats and infrastructure. A National Bureau of Economic Research study found that 89% of executives reported AI had “no impact on labor productivity.” ​

Companies have real reasons to be excited about AI, but those that use it to gain a competitive advantage and add real value will invest in the governance and infrastructure needed to operationalize these models effectively at scale. As Forbes contributor Güney Yıldız reports: “AI spend does not become ROI simply because usage goes up. Value capture requires workflow redesign, not just license distribution.”​

Here’s how forward-thinking leaders can redesign workflows to achieve real ROI from their AI investments.

AI should deliver tangible outcomes like making work easier, better or cheaper. Its purpose is not, as many leaders mistakenly assume, to simply increase AI adoption or add another tool to the technology stack.​

Executives can be forgiven for misunderstanding that point. Adoption can feel like action, and they face immense pressure to act. In reality, enterprises have different teams, roles and workflows, each with its own needs. Some can benefit from an AI tool or autonomous agent while others really don’t.

Rather than forcing an AI tool or agentic layer into every process, match AI capabilities to a specific problem. Right now, many businesses conflate success with usage. However, as the tokenmaxxing debacle shows, measuring usage isn’t the same as promoting real impact.

Instead of just measuring AI use, audit workflow bottlenecks before selecting tools so their capabilities match the problem they’re trying to solve. At the same time, prioritize tools that embed directly into existing systems, so workflows stay integrated and frictionless. If a tool can’t integrate directly with CRM, ERP or other core systems of record, its organizational impact will be limited.

The enterprise technology stack is already crowded with companies deploying hundreds of apps and SaaS solutions. Many work independently, disconnected from the disparate app ecosystem surrounding companies big and small. Adding new AI tools to this mix has limited impact and can even create more work for employees. Effective AI adoption that justifies AI spend will go beyond tools that answer questions or generate generic content. It will involve AI solutions that can proactively identify opportunities, recommend actions and even execute work. ​

For example, in marketing, where AI ad spending alone will top $32 billion in 2026, effective AI adoption could mean onboarding a solution that detects campaign performance issues, identifies underappreciated opportunities across a campaign or helps implement improvements to existing campaign collateral.

To maximize AI’s impact, invest in tools that make this possible and clarify the human element. Clearly define when AI can act independently, when approval is required and when humans must take the lead. ​

Combining the right tools with the right purpose in structured workflows, with clear roles and responsibilities, is the best way to invest in AI that gets work done.

AI is only as useful as the information and context it can access. Without clean, unified and reliable data, outputs can be inaccurate, inconsistent or disconnected from business priorities. Before making significant AI investments, smart enterprises will focus on organizing the technology they already have, connecting systems and simplifying workflows so AI can operate within business realities.​

Focus on infrastructure that connects AI to relevant business data, organizational knowledge and workflows while respecting role-based permissions and account-level boundaries.​

Understandably, security is foundational to these efforts. It can’t be bolted on later or retroactively applied. A governed environment, or “sandbox,” is a good place to start. Here, businesses can define what AI can access, what actions it can take and when it needs human approval.​

Customers aren’t inherently impressed by a company’s AI strategy, and neither are boards or shareholders. Everyone is looking for results.

That’s why the competitive advantage comes from how well organizations connect AI to their data, people, processes and business goals. It’s the product of organizations that build the right foundation, enabling AI to do the right work with the right context and under the right controls.

Investing in these fundamentals may not make headlines, but it’s the AI infrastructure bet that smart enterprises are making to deliver lasting business value.​

Diana Shipping Inc., founded in 1972 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange since 2005, operates a fleet of 36 dry bulk vessels, one of which is mortgage free. Our fleet has an average age of 12.9 years and a total deadweight capacity of approximately 4.1 million tonnes. We anticipate the delivery of 2 methanol dual-fuel newbuilding Kamsarmax dry bulk vessels at the end of 2027 and early 2028, respectively.

Fleet utilization reached 99.7% for the 9 months ended September 30, 2026, highlighting our effective vessel management strategy. As of the end of the third quarter, we employed 933 individuals at sea and ashore. Financially, our net total debt, including finance liabilities, less cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash divided by vessels market value stands at 32% as of September 30, 2026. This is supported by $217 million of cash reserves as of quarter end and total secured revenues of approximately $155 million as of November 17, 2026. Moving on to Slide 6. Dave Van der Linden: Thank you, Maria. And again, welcome to the participants on this latest quarterly earnings call from Diana Shipping, Inc. Looking at Slide 15 for a brief dry bulk market overview. We see that the third quarter proved to be the strongest quarter for the dry bulk market in several years. The softening we saw at the start of the quarter turned out to be short-lived and rates moved higher through August and September with the Baltic Dry Index reaching in early September, its highest level since 2021. The factors supporting the market remain largely the same: longer ton miles, historically low sailing speeds due to elevated bunker prices, trade disruptions caused by geopolitical conflicts and very limited demolition.

Capesize vessels once again outperformed Q3 earnings averaging $44,872 based on the 182 5TC Index, which was 13% higher than the second quarter and close to 60% higher than the third quarter of last year. In the period market, the 1-year rate for a 182 Index type without scrubber peaked at around $38,000 a day in mid-September and currently stands at around $36,000 a day and the rate for a modern Kamsarmax is around $19,500 a day and a modern Ultramax about $19,000 a day for a year, with shorter period fixtures for modern Ultramaxes in the Far East being concluded at significantly higher levels. The market remains heavily influenced by significant geopolitical and trade disruptions. The Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed. And at the same time, the attacks on ports, ships, infrastructure in the Black Sea has been escalating since July and has added an extra layer of risk and insecurity.

Bunker prices remain elevated and fuel availability remains tight in several locations east of Suez. As a result, vessel speeds remain at or near historical lows. If we move to Slide 16, we see the key demand drivers. The Capesize sector was supported by steady Australian iron ore flows and the continued ramp-up of Simandou. Q3 Pilbara exports were fairly flat year-on-year. However, Simandou is on track to export around 50 million to 60 million tonnes this year, which is already nearly half of its maximum capacity. Clarksons estimates 2026 seaborne iron ore trade to be at approximately 1.675 billion tonnes, which is up 2% from 2024. But more importantly, the average distance continues to increase at a larger rate.

The Guinean bauxite exports reached also 50 million tonnes in Q3. As expected, there was a slight dip compared to the previous quarter due to the rainy season, but it's still around 27% higher than Q3 last year, bringing exports for the first 9 months to nearly 165 million tonnes. You may remember that we mentioned in our last call, the possible export limit of the Guinean government, which is still possibly in place and which may cause a little bit of a drop of export volumes towards the end of the year. The Kamsarmax and Ultramax sectors remain supported by grain and coal.

Brazil set a new soybean record for exports of nearly 110 million tons shipped for the first 10 months of this year, which is up 8% year-on-year and already more than the full year of 2025. China imported 86 million tonnes of soybeans in the first 9 months, in line with last year with Brazil remaining the dominant source. And then on coal, China imported 353 million metric tons in the first 9 months, which was slightly up year-on-year. However, September imports were 5.6% lower than a year earlier as high domestic inventories and supply constraints in Indonesia weighed on volumes.

However, outside China, disrupted LNG supply from the Middle East continues to support coal-fired generation and long-haul coal flows, including from the U.S. Interesting to note is a significant increase in Chinese exports for dry bulk, not just steel, but also cement, clinker, fertilizers. These volumes have doubled since 2020, and this has mainly benefited the geared trade, which helps explain the Ultramax strength relative to the Kamsarmax vessels. It is also worth noting the strong demand growth in Southeast Asia, where imports have increased by more than 10% so far this year across a variety of commodities.

Indonesia and Vietnam are the main drivers and the IMF forecast Southeast Asian GDP growth at a healthy 4.9% for 2026 and 4.7% for 2027, Vietnam being -- having projected the strongest growth in the region at 8.4% this year. Overall, Clarksons forecast seaborne dry bulk trade to grow by 2.3% in tons in 2026, but 4.1% in ton miles. Moving to Slide 17 for the supply outlook. According to industry estimates, the bulk carrier fleet stood at around 1.1 billion tonne deadweight at the end of September and deliveries in the first 9 months reached around 32 million deadweight. Net fleet growth was 2.8% year-to-date with full year 2026 growth expected to be around 3.6%.

For Capes, fleet growth was limited, seeing only 37 Capes and Newcastlemaxes delivered in the first 9 months versus 152 Kamsarmaxes and 168 Ultramax vessels. The bulk carrier order book, however, now stands nearly at 15% of the existing fleet, which is up from around 13% at the time of our last call, mainly due to heavy Capesize and Newcastlemax fleet ordering, which now represents 23% of the existing fleet. 13% of the Kamsarmax and Panamax fleet is on order and 15% of the Ultramax/Supramax fleet is still on order. Ship recycling remains extremely low. According to BIMCO, only 70 bulkers of 3 million tonne deadweight in total were recycled between January and October.

This is 36% lower year-on-year, the lowest level in 18 years, and it confirms that the 5 million tonne deadweight of scrapping, which was expected at the beginning of the year will not be reached. And then to finalize Slide 18. Let's conclude with the main positive and negative factors that analysts expect could influence the dry bulk market going forward. On the positive side, ton-mile demand remains supportive with 2026 growth forecast at 4.1%, above projected fleet growth of 3.9%. Long-haul Atlantic to Asia iron ore and bauxite trades continue to support Capesize and Newcastlemax utilization. Grain exports from the Americas and selected trade routing will help Panamax and geared vessel employment.

Operating speeds will remain at near historical lows while dry docking and geopolitical disruption absorbs effective capacity and demolition is expected to remain limited, but the aging fleet and firm recycling prices could, at some point, provide medium-term scrapping potential. On the negative side, fleet growth is expected to accelerate in 2026, especially for Capes. BIMCO forecast 2027 supply growth of 3% to 4% against demand growth of 0.5% to 2.5%, depending on whether and how long the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed. Chinese steel output is declining, which could weigh on iron ore demand, while China's coal imports have started to soften on high inventories.

Policy risk, especially in Guinea, where export controls are expected to slow bauxite shipments as well as in China and Indonesia. Geopolitical uncertainty remains high, prolonged high energy prices could hurt global growth and a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz or a full return to the Red Sea would release tonnage and shorten trade routes. And on this note, I will pass the call back to our CEO, Ms. Semiramis Paliou, for some important takeaway points from this earnings call. Thank you very much.

#2985. Why Nutanix Plunged Today

A solid headline earnings beat wasn't enough to offset other uncertainties, including a CEO transition.

By Billy Duberstein – Nov 25, 2026 at 1:28PM EST

Shares of virtualization software company Nutanix (NTNX -15.19%) plunged 17.7% on Wednesday as of 1:24 p.m. EDT.

Nutanix released its fiscal first-quarter 2027 earnings last night, exceeding expectations. However, the company also announced that its current CEO is stepping down, a move that surprised investors.

The CEO transition, combined with some imperfections in key underlying metrics and a bearish market mood, conspired to drive today's big sell-off.

In the first fiscal quarter, Nutanix's revenue increased 15.2% to $772.4 million, while adjusted (non-GAAP) earnings per share grew 78.0% to $0.73. Both figures beat analysts' expectations.

Nevertheless, there were some imperfections in the quarter and in forward guidance. Management forecast a decline in the company's operating margin in the fiscal year ahead, even as it raised the figure from its prior guidance. According to management, the company is going to invest more heavily in research and development and salespeople, in what it described as a "significant" reinvestment into AI and agentic capabilities.

Additionally, the company's bookings, which reflect the value of total deals that have yet to be converted to revenue, fell 2% from the year-ago quarter. While management chalked this up to just a few large delayed deals and the company allocating resources differently, investors were in an unforgiving mood.

Finally, CEO Rajiv Ramaswami announced he would step down from the position he has held for about six years and would stay on to help appoint his successor, ensuring a smooth transition. While this seems like an orderly CEO transition and has nothing to do with performance issues or other concerns, the uncertainty about Nutanix’s leadership augmented all the other worries.

The large investment behind agentic applications, the slight decrease in bookings, and the CEO transition weren't necessarily bright red flags that anything is wrong with Nutanix. However, the combination of all these factors, along with the extremely bearish sentiment toward tech stocks today, conspired to cause the big drop in Nutanix stock.

This sell-off may very well be overdone, making today's drop a buying opportunity. Nutanix stock now trades at under 20 times this year's projected adjusted earnings per share. The company has a healthy cash balance on its balance sheet, and its virtualization software is likely to remain in demand as enterprises manage data across public and private clouds.

However, this underlying uncertainty may remain until Nutanix finally lands a new CEO, which could take months.

TL;DR: Rising inflation could, counterintuitively, help push mortgage rates further down.

Mortgage rates are a little lower this morning, and where they'll go next isn't totally clear.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.05% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is eight basis points lower than yesterday and 33 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Inflation data out this morning looks, at first glance, like bad news for mortgage rates. But depending on how markets react, we could actually see lower mortgage rates. Keep reading after the charts for all the details.

Below are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for perspective.

P.S. Markets will be closed tomorrow for Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, and mortgage rates don't move much when the markets aren't moving. I won't be here to talk to you about mortgage rates, either, 'cause NerdWallet gives us Thursday and Friday off. Happy Thanksgiving!

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Like I mentioned above, it's not totally obvious where mortgage rates will head next. Let's walk through the two scenarios.

Here's why rates could go up: This morning, we got October's Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, also known as PCE. It's the last measure of inflation to come out each month, but it's also the Federal Reserve's preferred metric, so PCE gets a lot of attention.

The stats came in mostly as predicted, though it's not like the predictions were good — inflation's been overly strong for a while. But the core year-over-year figure, which came in a tenth of a percent over predictions, could prove troublesome. Core PCE removes categories that can be extra volatile, so it's considered a measure that shows the underlying trend. In this case, the underlying trend is Not Good.

It's already pretty much a lock that we'll see a rate hike at the Federal Reserve's December meeting, because yes, raising the federal funds rate is the Fed's main tool for taming inflation. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but a rate-hiking cycle from the central bankers definitely keeps upward pressure on borrowing costs.

On the other hand, here's why that same inflation data could help rates go down: Over the past several days, we've watched the stock market go on a wild ride, with the Anthropic IPO and the return of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Yesterday, things weren't looking good for tech stocks, and these inflation numbers could make it even worse.

The amount that tech companies have borrowed to fund AI buildout is a significant concern for investors, since companies will have to cover those costs before investors see any profits. It's already a big task, and if everything costs more thanks to inflation, it's that much harder.

This AI-related anxiety is rough on the stock market, but it's been a boon for Treasury bonds. More demand for bonds pushes up bond prices, which brings down bond yields (basically, the return investors get on a bond). Mortgage rates for 30-year loans are generally benchmarked to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, so here's why you care about all of this: Lower Treasury yields means lower mortgage rates, too. If investors keep stressing about inflation eating into tech profits, we could see mortgage rates continue to move lower.

That was a lot of info on inflation, but inflation's not the only major metric influencing rates.

Let's back up for a second. The Federal Reserve tries to keep the economy steady by focusing on two key goals, often referred to as the Fed's dual mandate. One side is price stability — keeping inflation reasonable. The other is maximum employment, meaning those who want to work are able to find jobs.

Next week we'll shift our focus to the employment side of the Federal Reserve's mandate, because the first week of the month is always all about employment data. On Tuesday, Dec. 1, we'll kick things off with the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS). JOLTS can tip us off to trends in the labor market; stuff like whether folks are leaving jobs voluntarily or if companies have openings that are going unfilled.

On Wednesday, payroll firm ADP will release its monthly employment stats. ADP is looking at its own payroll data to get an idea of how the job market is growing or contracting. The numbers don't include the public sector, but ADP often provides a preview of how the jobs report will go.

The Employment Situation Summary, better known as the jobs report, drops on Friday. This is the big one, since it tells us the nation's unemployment rate. The jobs report's other major stat is, similar to ADP, how many jobs the economy added or lost in the previous month. Unlike ADP though, the jobs report is inclusive of everybody in the public and private sectors.

Lately the labor market's been looking super healthy, which is great news for the economy but less positive for mortgage rates. When hiring's strong, the Fed can feel safer raising the federal funds rate (that's the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers adjust). Higher rates tend to discourage businesses from borrowing and expanding, so if the job market's on shaky footing, the central bankers are going to be cautious about raising the benchmark rate.

What we're seeing now though, where inflation is clearly the problem and employment's just fine, is a recipe for higher rates. Again, the Fed doesn't control mortgage rates, but the central bank being in rate-hike mode puts upward pressure on mortgage rates.

If we were to see employment falter in this latest round of numbers, it still probably wouldn't change the Fed's plan. That would be one poor month for the labor market versus months upon months of inflation running rampant — so yeah, they'll keep an eye on jobs, but inflation's still the scourge.

Our most likely source of lower mortgage rates in the short term is what I described above; investors who are leery of inflation and the promise of AI looking to the safe harbor of the bond market.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you could start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.55% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

#2980. How Legacy Data Pipelines Become A Liability When AI Moves From Chat To Action

Prashanthi Kolluru is the founder of KloudPortal. Helping global capability centers (GCCs) hire product-ready engineering pods.

In enterprise data engineering initiatives, I’ve noticed an often-overlooked pattern: a data pipeline can be judged successful simply because it runs as expected. Data moves between systems, scheduled jobs complete, reports are delivered and the business keeps operating smoothly. Yet the same pipeline may rely on assumptions about data freshness, transformation logic, quality and business rules that become challenging to manage as requirements evolve.​

This is becoming increasingly significant as enterprises move from AI assistants that retrieve information to agents that execute tasks. An AI agent operating within an enterprise workflow may use incorrect information to update records, initiate processes or influence business decisions without anyone realizing it.​

This shift has prompted me to examine more closely the weaknesses that may have been manageable in traditional analytics environments but become more critical when AI is integrated into operational workflows.

Five areas deserve particular attention before organizations extend AI agents into consequential workflows.

A pipeline that refreshes data overnight may be perfectly adequate for a historical sales report. It can be unsuitable for an agent making decisions that depend on current inventory, account balances or order status.

The risk depends on the business decision, not simply on how old the data is. A delay of several hours may have little impact on one workflow and materially change the outcome of another.

Technology leaders should define acceptable data freshness for each AI use case. Some workflows may need event-driven updates; others may work with scheduled processing. Rebuilding every pipeline for real-time delivery is rarely necessary. The goal is to match data availability to the consequences of acting on it.

Legacy pipelines often rely on scripts and mappings that embed source-specific assumptions and business rules. When engineers introduce a new system or data source, they may need to modify multiple parts of the pipeline and retest downstream dependencies.

This becomes harder as AI agents need information from more enterprise systems and business context changes more frequently.

Metadata-driven pipeline architecture offers one way to reduce this maintenance burden. Source mappings, transformation rules, validation checks and load configurations can be managed as metadata that a reusable framework interprets. This can make changes easier to manage than repeatedly modifying hard-coded procedures.

Metadata alone, however, does not guarantee flexibility. Business rules still need clear ownership, version control and testing. Otherwise, an organization simply moves its complexity from code into configuration.

A missing field or duplicate record in a dashboard may be noticed during a review. The same defect, consumed by an AI agent, could influence a subsequent workflow before a person examines the underlying data.

Consider customer records that use inconsistent identifiers across systems. An agent combining those records could associate an instruction with the wrong account if the pipeline fails to resolve the inconsistency.

Validation therefore needs to go beyond checking whether a pipeline completed successfully. Teams should test completeness, uniqueness, relationships between records, acceptable ranges and relevant business rules. Where checks fail, the system should flag or quarantine affected data rather than silently passing it downstream.

The appropriate controls depend on the use case, but the principle is consistent: successful data movement is not proof of trustworthy data.

When an AI-assisted workflow produces an unexpected result, teams need to establish which source records were used, how those records were transformed and which business definitions applied at the time.

That investigation becomes difficult when dependencies are undocumented, transformations are scattered across scripts or data definitions differ between systems. Without reliable lineage, teams may struggle to reproduce an outcome or identify where an error entered the pipeline.

Organizations should maintain traceable data flows, versioned transformations and monitoring that connects pipeline failures to downstream use cases. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework can also help teams structure their approach to identifying, assessing and managing AI-related risks.

For workflows with significant business consequences, treat the ability to reconstruct the data path as an operational requirement, not merely a documentation exercise. ​

A pipeline may deliver accurate account information to an agent, but access to that information should not automatically authorize the agent to initiate a payment, change a customer record or approve a transaction.

These are separate decisions: what data a system can read, what actions it can perform and which actions require human approval.

As organizations connect agents to enterprise applications, they should define permissions around specific operations, use appropriate controls for higher-risk actions and retain audit trails of what the agent accessed and did. Access policies should apply to the agent’s identity and the workflow it operates within, not simply to the data source.

Data engineering and AI governance need to work together here. A well-governed pipeline cannot compensate for unrestricted action permissions, just as a tightly controlled agent cannot make unreliable data trustworthy. ​

Modernizing a legacy data environment does not necessarily mean replacing every pipeline or moving every workload to real-time processing. It starts with understanding which data feeds support AI workflows and what can happen when those feeds are delayed, incomplete or incorrect.

Can technology leaders assess those pipelines against five practical questions: Is the data fresh enough for the decision? Are transformations understandable and maintainable? Are quality failures detected before the data is used? Can you reconstruct the source and transformation history? Are data permissions and agent action permissions clearly separated?

Enterprises should avoid treating AI readiness as a separate layer added on top of existing data infrastructure. Pipeline design, maintenance and governance will influence what AI agents can safely do with enterprise information.

Organizations should examine these foundations early in AI planning rather than discover their limitations after agents become embedded in critical workflows. Modernization should reflect the business consequences of each use case and give AI agents a dependable basis for action.

#2977. Ready for ‘The Great Lock In’? Viral Money Trend Can Improve Focus

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Winter is the ideal time to make progress on your financial goals.

When it’s cold outside, it’s the ideal time to stay home, organize your finances, set some new money goals and make progress toward them.

That’s the promise of the viral winter money trend known as “The Great Lock In” that’s circulating on social media.

“You’re probably not doing too much,” says Robert Baird, wealth manager at Cornerstone Financial Services in Southfield, Michigan. “It gets dark early. So those can be great months to lock into saving and not spend in excess.”

One important component of the Great Lock In is developing new routines that will last well into 2027, says Jordan Mangaliman, founder and fiduciary wealth advisor at GoldLine Wealth Management in Fullerton, California.

“We want a long-term habit versus a Band-Aid fix,” he says. “In today’s economy, money goes in and out so blindingly fast.”

Ready to join the movement? Here’s how to get started.

What’s your money moonshot? Maybe it’s paying off all your credit card debt or purchasing a home. Or spending less than you earn. Defining it is the first step toward achieving it.

“Spend a lot of time identifying what that goal is,” Baird says. “Everyone’s in a different position, so comparing yourself to what you see online might not be applicable.”

Even while setting ambitious money goals, it’s worth grounding them in reality, Mangaliman says.

If you want to save a larger portion of your income, he suggests trying the new saving pattern for a couple of months to see how it feels rather than saying you’ll do it forever and then getting frustrated.

“It’s a marathon, not a sprint,” Mangaliman adds.

Once you’ve outlined those big goals for your Great Lock In, create a budget to help you achieve them, Baird says.

He suggests combing through your previous credit or debit card spending to see where your money is going. Then you can decide what you want to change or shift. Using a tool like the 50/30/20 budget calculator can also help. This approach allots 50% of take-home pay toward needs, 30% toward wants and 20% toward savings and debt payments beyond the minimum.

Baird suggests including saving as a line item in your budget so you don’t forget to do it. “Building that cost into your budget will put you in a better position later,” he says.

Any Great Lock In should include growing your savings, because that makes achieving other goals easier, Baird says.

“Maybe there’s something you could cut in the short term to build up that savings,” he says. Good targets include subscription services, food delivery, entertainment and travel costs.

Saving more is especially challenging in today’s environment, when everyday expenses like gas are higher than they were a year ago.

Baird says that makes winter a good time to try to reduce costs. There can be fewer temptations to go out and spend money when the days are shorter and the temperatures are colder.

Mangaliman recommends setting aside three to six months’ worth of expenses, although even a smaller amount is helpful. “Ultimately it’s about what you can afford,” he says. “It’s the foundation of your financial house.”

Along with building savings, paying down high-interest debt is another pillar of the Great Lock In.

With credit card interest rates higher than they were a few years ago, carrying credit card debt has gotten more expensive. “I would consider applying some savings to paying down debt, especially right now when your debt is costing you more than you can earn in savings,” Baird says. (You still want to reserve an emergency fund to cover unexpected expenses.)

“High-interest debt is one of the biggest thieves of wealth,” Mangaliman says. And one way to avoid turning to debt again in the future is to build up that emergency fund so it’s there for you if you need it.

Even when you are committed to a Great Lock In, some hiccups along the way are inevitable. Success depends on continuing anyway.

“It’s like a diet,” Baird says. “Just because you ate ice cream on a Sunday doesn’t mean on Monday you can’t go right back to being disciplined again.”

“Be kind to yourself and do everything in moderation,” Mangaliman suggests. Just wanting to improve your finances is already a great first step, he says.

In fact, he embraces the Great Lock In mentality himself. “There’s an old saying: It’s not how you start, but how you finish,” he says. “And you want to finish the year on a strong note so you carry those habits into 2027 and beyond.”

#2976. Cross-Functional Collaboration Is Fashion’s New Competitive Advantage

Maximilien Abadie, Deputy CEO and a member of the Executive Committee, Lectra.

​Speed and creativity have always been defining features of the fashion industry. In a climate marked by fragmentation and continuing volatility, accelerating time to market and achieving the all-important five R’s (right place, right product, right price, right quantities and right consumer) have become less about moving faster at individual stages and more about improving how information is shared and decisions are made across the value chain.

Companies that create the digital and cultural infrastructure to support cross-functional collaboration make it possible to unify workflows, anticipate challenges earlier and share data for faster, better decisions. This transforms the way a company creates, manufactures and sells their products. ​

Every product that makes it to market is shaped by contributions from hundreds of different individuals, many of whom do not speak the same language or share a common perspective. The linear, step-by-step approach to collection development—design followed by development, then production and ending with marketing, merchandising and e-commerce—struggles to provide the agility needed to respond quickly to the dynamism that characterizes this industry.

When design, production and sales teams work as separate entities, each with their own tools, data and objectives, decision-making is slower and inefficiencies are greater. A feasibility issue discovered in production could have been identified at the development stage. Consumer insights gathered during the marketing phase are not passed on to creative teams. These disconnects can result in missed sales opportunities, excess inventory and frustrated customers. ​

Cross-functional collaboration supported by shared data contributes to greater resilience, innovation and growth. Research shows that cross-functional, team-focused transformations can drive a 30% increase in efficiency. When information flows freely across an interconnected value chain, decisions happen faster, errors are identified earlier and fewer resources are wasted.

One of the most tangible benefits of data-based collaboration is its impact on time to market, which remains a critical challenge for global fashion brands. While some fashion players can develop and launch products in a matter of days, others still operate on timelines of six to nine months. Closing this gap requires rethinking product development from the earliest creative stages and ensuring continuity of information across the entire product life cycle.

Beyond improving collaboration, these solutions help preserve and scale expertise by making institutional knowledge, technical know-how and historical product data accessible across the organization. Along with accelerating onboarding and decision-making, this helps brands ensure that valuable expertise is retained and leveraged across generations of teams.

Data-based collaboration requires a shared infrastructure capable of integrating multiple functions and partners. Solutions embedded with AI and digitalization are the key enablers of this transformation. While product life cycle management (PLM) solutions remain essential for product data management, governance and life cycle visibility, a new generation of AI-enabled product development solutions is emerging to support the day-to-day workflow of bringing a product from concept to production.

By bringing together internal teams, as well as a brand’s global network of suppliers, subcontractors and partners, these solutions ensure that all stakeholders are aligned and working from the same up-to-date information. Companies can capture and communicate data on designs, tech packs, materials, costs, timelines and suppliers in a common framework that cross-functional teams can rely on as products progress.

When each team member has a 360-degree vision of the product in its journey, there are fewer surprises and improved coordination.

The case for shared data infrastructure becomes even more urgent in light of upcoming traceability and sustainability regulations. The Digital Product Passport (DPP), part of the European Union’s Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation, will require products sold in the EU in 2027 to carry structured, standardized product information. Even in the early phase of implementation, which will be a minimal, simplified version of the digital product passport, companies will be expected to provide data on material composition, origin, carbon footprint, supply chain traceability, recyclability, care, durability and chemical compliance.

Compliance will require alignment across the full product cycle. While the first phase will most likely only require supply chain traceability up to Tier 1 and Tier 2 suppliers, adopting a digital traceability approach that starts with the original fibers that will eventually be used in garments and other products provides the foundation for visibility across all tiers of the supply chain. Artificial intelligence is a key enabler of this tracing technology. It continuously monitors transactions to detect inconsistencies or fraudulent claims, enabling brands to move from theoretical commitments to proven actions. Companies that build this infrastructure now will be positioned to leverage transparency as a competitive advantage.

Collaborative solutions are reshaping how work is organized, executed and experienced. Beyond enabling basic communication, they support new ways of working that emphasize shared visibility and consistency across teams. In a business environment increasingly characterized by volatility, complexity and rapid change, these platforms are becoming an important enabler for companies seeking to operate more efficiently and quickly.
