#2973. When Days Matter: Navigating The AI-Accelerated Exploit Lifecycle

Eoin Keary Founder & CEO of Edgescan, an enterprise CTEM (Continuous Testing and Exposure Management platform) used by Fortune 500s.

​AI is fundamentally changing the velocity of the threat landscape, particularly the time between vulnerability discovery and weaponization. Vulnerabilities that historically took months, or even up to a year, to become active exploits can now move into the wild within days. AI also expands the attack surface itself as organizations deploy AI systems and agents across their environments, including systems that may not be fully visible to security teams.​

This creates a new imperative: Security processes designed around periodic assessment and remediation must evolve to operate at the speed of continuous change. They should consider a different approach to security that employs AI to manage data volume while retaining a human in the loop for critical decision making. In this way, their organizations can rise with the tide of AI-driven threats by purifying their cybersecurity data to ensure it remains manageable and actionable.​

The fundamental challenge in vulnerability management has never been finding vulnerabilities but determining which findings represent genuine, actionable risk. Organizations must distinguish between false positives, vulnerabilities that are real but not exploitable and vulnerabilities that are exploitable but mitigated by other controls.​

Only after those layers of validation can security teams determine which remaining vulnerabilities represent the greatest business risk and should be addressed first. AI threatens to amplify the existing “vulnerability noise” problem by dramatically increasing the volume of findings entering the security team’s workflow. The answer can’t be asking already-constrained security and development teams to manually process an increasingly powerful “firehose” of alerts.​

Slowing down detection isn’t the answer. A better answer is to add a validation layer between detection and action. The value of continuous assessment is its ability to provide a more current view of the environment. Without validation, however, it just produces more noise, faster. This is especially important as AI accelerates both vulnerability discovery and vulnerability exploitation.

The temptation to use AI to automate remediation and allow systems to patch vulnerabilities without human intervention is obvious.​ Yet autonomous remediation can introduce significant operational risk when an AI system lacks the business context necessary to understand the consequences of its actions. AI should be used to make security professionals “more bionic,” processing information, accelerating analysis and supporting decisions, while humans retain responsibility for critical remediation decisions.​

As for technical vulnerability data, it alone is insufficient to determine what an organization should fix first. Effective prioritization requires context about the affected asset, its criticality, its role in the business, its data flows and the potential consequences of exploitation. AI can help organizations apply and process this context at scale, but only if the underlying security data is accurate, validated and meaningful.

For teams already buried in findings, the promise of less noise is appealing. The questions start when we discuss what adopting it involves. How much of their time will we need? Will it work with their existing tools? Will the findings arriving on their desks actually be any better?

In conversations with customers and prospective clients, these are always understandable concerns. They’ve heard plenty of promises about making security simpler. They want to know how much work it’ll take to get started and how much work it’ll save them afterwards. Sending over a mountain of alerts and wishing the team good luck is a fairly generous interpretation of helping.

Providers need to be clear about who does the work. If we offer validated findings, the validation is our responsibility. It’s important to establish which findings are real and investigate exploitability and assess relevant controls before passing the results to the customer.

Trust is another hurdle. Fewer findings can sound suspicious when the industry has spent years presenting bigger numbers as evidence of a better job. Customers need to see why something has been ruled out or deprioritized, what testing supports that decision and what remains uncertain.

“AI said so” isn’t an explanation I’d fancy taking into a board meeting. Show the evidence and let people challenge the conclusion.​

Yes, cost always comes up, but the subscription is only part of the calculation. Investigating false positives, chasing findings that can’t be reproduced and passing inconclusive tickets between teams all costs money. Those hours don’t become free because they’re missing from the procurement spreadsheet. Providers must demonstrate the reduction in effort for the client and explain the price they charge.

The practical route is to start with a defined scope and agree what success looks like with security development and the budget owner. Measure the time spent investigating findings, the quality of evidence reaching developers and how quickly confirmed risks receive attention. Make implementation manageable, work with existing systems and show the results. That gives each team a reason to support adoption.​​

Organizations need greater visibility into their attack surface and a continuous understanding of what they’re trying to secure. Continuous assessment and visibility will become increasingly important as the pace of vulnerability discovery and exploitation accelerates. However, continuous assessment inevitably creates more data, making validation and suppression of irrelevant or low-value findings increasingly important.

Organizations should prioritize security approaches that continuously assess the environment while filtering, validating and contextualizing findings before they reach security and development teams. The ultimate objective isn’t to automate every security decision but to ensure that even as the volume of cybersecurity data grows exponentially, organizations can reduce that information to a manageable number of accurate, contextual and actionable risks.​

In an AI-accelerated threat landscape, the organizations best positioned to respond will be those that can rise with the tide by purifying their cybersecurity data rather than drowning in it.​​

#2972. Billionaire David Tepper Just Loaded Up on SpaceX Stock. Should You Follow His Lead?

SpaceX looks like a bargain buy right now.

By Keithen Drury – Nov 25, 2026 at 1:33PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›

Checking in to see what the billionaire hedge fund managers do is a smart investment strategy. While you shouldn't blindly follow all their moves, using them for idea generation is a smart plan.

One billionaire hedge fund I follow is Appaloosa Management, run by David Tepper. During Q3, he loaded up on Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.07%) shares. He owned barely any at the end of Q2 (SpaceX went public right before Q2 ended), but as of the end of Q3, it was the fourth-largest position in his portfolio, accounting for nearly 8% of its value. That shows extreme confidence in the stock, but should you follow suit and open a position in it?

One major reason retail investors should not blindly copy the moves of billionaire hedge fund managers is that the information we are getting is well out of date by the time we see it. Investment fund managers only have to report their end-of-quarter holdings in their 13F filings, so the purchases involved could have happened at any time during a quarter. And those forms don’t get filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission until 45 days after the quarter they cover has ended. So any given stock move described in those forms could be more than four months old by the time news of it reaches the general public.

During Q3, SpaceX traded as low as $110 per share and as high as $160 per share at the start of the quarter. It ended the quarter around $151 per share — just above its opening-day first trading price. Today's price of about $130 per share is right in the middle of the Q3 range where Tepper could have bought. So investors don't have to worry too much about overpaying for the stock, as it's on sale relative to where it traded for most of Q3.

Additionally, by waiting to buy until now, you have more information than Tepper had available in Q3, and that information is quite bullish.

Although SpaceX is generally recognized as a space exploration company, it's increasingly an artificial intelligence investment. Its AI segment now accounts for over half of its revenue, and has grown at a 213% pace year over year last quarter. That's an impressive growth rate, and according to CEO Elon Musk, it's only going to get better.

During the Q3 conference call, Musk asserted that SpaceX's annual recurring revenue could rise to somewhere in the $500 billion to $1 trillion range by the end of next year, thanks to its booming AI division. While Musk is no stranger to making bold projections that don't always pan out, the bigger idea here is that there will be monster AI growth in 2027 that investors need to prepare for. With SpaceX becoming more AI-focused, I think it's a smart pick in this space.

Investors should take advantage of the current price of SpaceX's stock and scoop up shares. Tepper may have been a bit early to the party by buying shares in Q3, but I think his decision was the right one.

#2968. 4 Ways to Prep Your Finances Before the Next Tech Outage

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

You don’t need a basement bunker, but keeping some cash on hand might help.

If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.

Have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year? Maybe.

But what about your money? If your area was hit by a natural disaster or your bank had an outage, are your finances ready?

Dan Stanush, senior financial planner at Charles Schwab in Asheville, North Carolina, recalls how fast financial conveniences disappeared after Hurricane Helene hit in 2024. “We lost power for three weeks and water for six weeks,” he said in an email. “And some local businesses could only accept cash or checks because card systems and ATMs were down.”

Don’t get caught unprepared. Here are the moves experts suggest to help you weather various types of emergencies:

Last week’s Chase outage was a good reminder that access to your bank balance can be disrupted. Stash at least enough cash at home — in small bills — to cover one week of expenses, says Jeff Judge, a certified financial planner (CFP) with Chesapeake Financial Planners in Forest Hill, Maryland.

If systems go down, ATMs can go down with them, said Eileen Olson, a CFP with Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina, in an email. Keeping cash in a safe at home is a good plan, but it’s also smart to carry cash when you travel. (Remember when planes were grounded nationwide a week and a half ago?)

“My parents and sister were traveling overseas on 9/11 and got stuck much longer than they expected,” Olson said. “After that, they always traveled with more cash.”

If your primary bank and its app were down, would you be able to pay bills? Having an account at more than one bank gives you an alternate funding source. Consider opening a high-yield savings account at a second bank or credit union for your emergency fund.

“This is the step I push hardest,” Judge says. “I had a client whose debit card, credit card and savings all ran through one bank, so when that bank’s system went down, she couldn’t even buy gas.”

If you don’t want to open a second bank account, a second credit card from a different bank and preferably on a different network (i.e. Visa vs. Mastercard) can provide another way to pay for things. “If there’s a problem with one credit card network, I have a backup with two other credit cards,” says Tony Steuer, author of “Get Ready! A Step-by-Step Planner for Maintaining Your Financial First Aid Kit.”

Make a printed list of your accounts, along with account numbers and key contact numbers. Include your bank, insurers, credit card companies and any financial professionals. Store the list with copies of essential paperwork, including insurance policies and their declarations pages, estate planning documents, legal certificates and identification — potentially in a fire-resistant file box.

Keep a digital copy of your documents in a password-protected, encrypted spot as well. A password manager can store all of your login info.

Joon Um, a CFP with Secure Tax & Accounting in Beverly Hills, California, suggests digital storage site Everplans to his clients, but there are a variety of sites that offer encrypted document storage.

Take some time to write down how you’d pay for groceries, gas and medication if your usual payment methods weren’t available. What expenses would you need to cover first? What recurring bills are on autopay? Where would you keep the cash and any key documents you’d want to take with you if you had to leave home? Make sure other household members know where everything is.

And set a reminder to update your records at regular intervals. Steuer, for instance, saves his account statements as PDFs and prints everything out once a year. “One of the big concerns is that people could conceivably break into your 401(k) and drain your 401(k) account,” he says. Account statements could help if a hack affects any financial balances.

It all adds up to a web of protection that (hopefully) you’ll never have to use.

“The goal is not to anticipate every scenario,” said Schwab's Dan Stanush, “but to have enough flexibility to meet basic needs while systems come back online.”

#2966. Is the Anthropic IPO to Blame for Bitcoin's Recent Downturn? The Answer Might Surprise You.

There's a finite amount of liquidity in the financial markets, and Bitcoin is often somewhat of a warehouse for it.

By Alex Carchidi – Nov 25, 2026 at 1:37PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

On Nov. 19, Anthropic (ANT +0.87%) became available to trade after raising a record $81.3 billion in its initial public offering (IPO), and just two days later, Bitcoin (BTC +0.97%) fell below its psychologically important $60,000 level to hit $55,130, its lowest since September 2024. For many investors, those events are connected, and Anthropic's debut is blamed for Bitcoin's poor performance.

In short, one prevailing theory on the topic says that legions of investors sold their crypto to buy shares of Anthropic, just as they seemed to be doing right before Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.07%)—better known as SpaceX—had its IPO in June. But does this narrative really hold up to scrutiny?

U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and their capital flows are important bellwethers for Bitcoin's price, as they indicate demand for Bitcoin in the traditional financial system.

Those ETFs saw $1.9 billion in net outflows from Nov. 5 to 13, and then another $1.8 billion from Nov. 16 to 20. By Nov. 23, November's outflows had reached $4.7 billion, a new record.

Analysts have been largely consistent in saying that the IPO-drain story is pretty unproven; 10x Research's Markus Thielen called the timing coincidental. Similarly, TDX Strategies' Dick Lo called the IPO one factor affecting Bitcoin, but not necessarily the primary one, and he pointed to hotter-than-expected inflation data and rising Treasury yields as more important causes. Outflows accelerated the week the offering closed on Nov. 20, and then continued through Nov. 23.

Market turbulence has also been bad for Bitcoin recently. In the week ending Nov. 20, U.S. stocks had their worst weekly performance since April 2025, due in part to the Federal Reserve's meeting minutes showing widespread support for more rate hikes, which tend to be bad for risky assets like cryptocurrencies. With Anthropic's stock now sinking, interest rates and economic uncertainty appear to be the bigger culprits.

Bitcoin's performance after the SpaceX IPO in June is a helpful data point for deciding whether to buy the dip here.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs saw a then-record $4.5 billion in net outflows that month, partly because the SpaceX IPO pulled capital away from crypto. Then, in July, they took in $403 million as the coin rose by 7.3%.

So money returned to Bitcoin, but only in a trickle, which coincided with a decent price rebound. The same could well happen once the market's attention turns away from Anthropic, potentially within the next few weeks.

Of course, one recent precedent isn't the same as a pattern.

Nothing about this IPO changes why people hold Bitcoin, so it still makes sense to buy slowly, in small amounts. Just be aware that if the Fed hikes interest rates further, it could be a long time before your Bitcoin purchases break even, and there could be a bit more downside in the near term.

#2963. Super Hi (HDL) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Southeast and East Asia held up as North America lagged on sales.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 25, 2026 at 1:37PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Super Hi (HDL +6.93%) reported a 7.1% year-over-year revenue increase for the third quarter, driven by higher guest traffic and an expanded restaurant network despite same-store sales pressure in North America. The company reported a significant increase in net profit due to nonoperating foreign exchange gains, while operating margins were impacted by phased investments in secondary brands and the centralization of management support functions. Management reported that Southeast Asia and East Asia remained resilient, whereas the North American market requires strategic adjustments to menu pricing and guest engagement to reach mainstream local diners. The company continues to advance its multi-brand strategy through the Pomegranate Plan and is leveraging digital tools to refine its loyalty program, which currently contributes 90% of restaurant revenue.

Operator: Hello, investors and analysts. Thank you so much for joining Super Hi International's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. With us today are Mr. Yu Li, Executive Director and CEO; and Ms. Lu Li, Chief Financial Officer and Joint Company Secretary. Today's call may contain forward-looking statements, including statements about our strategy, business plans and outlook. The information we present today and our comments and answers to your questions reflect management's views as of today. Please refer to the latest safe harbor statement in our earnings release, which also applies to this call. The call will be conducted in Mandarin with simultaneous English interpretation provided by an external provider. In the event of any discrepancy, the Chinese remarks will prevail.

Today's slides are available on our Investor Relations website. Now I'll turn the call over to Mr. Yu Li, our CEO and Executive Director, to review our third quarter 2026 results.

Yu Li: Thank you. Hello, investors and analysts. I'm Yu Li, CEO and Executive Director of Super Hi International. Let me walk you through our operating performance for the third quarter of 2026. This quarter, we stayed with our long-term strategy of focusing on both employees and guests. We worked to improve the guest experience, refine our menu and manage each restaurant more closely. Haidilao restaurants served 8.4 million guest visits, up 3.7% year-over-year. Both overall and same-store average table turnover reached 4x per day, up 0.1 turn each. Haidilao restaurant revenue rose by 2.4%. We also continue to grow revenue beyond dine-in and advance our Pomegranate Plan. Combined revenue from delivery and other businesses grew by 78.2% year-over-year.

That helped lift total revenue to $229 million, up 7.1% year-over-year and 4.8% quarter-over-quarter. Operating profit was $9.933 million with an operating margin of 4.3%. As we improved operations at existing restaurants, we also continued to expand our network. We opened 3 Haidilao restaurants and began putting resources in place for upcoming openings. We continue to explore additional brands and strengthen our shared support functions at headquarters. Related investment at this stage was higher than a year ago. Operating profit improved from the second quarter, but remained below the prior-year level. Let me walk you through our main initiatives this quarter. First, we stayed focused on restaurant operations and adapted guest engagement and staff management to each market.

We continue to give regions and restaurants flexibility. Local teams could adjust how they operated based on local spending conditions, their guest mix and each restaurant's performance. We also stepped up frontline training, staffing and day-to-day management. As preparations for new openings progressed, we began recruiting and training for key roles in advance. To date, more than 60% of our restaurants have trained managers ready to step up. That gives us a talent pipeline for new openings and ongoing operations. In guest engagement, we put more weight on how much a campaign actually drives traffic and repeat visits alongside discounts it offers.

Take Vietnam, our restaurants improved loyalty benefits, engaged staff to bring in new guests and maintained closer ties with guest communities. They also ran campaigns around local holidays and dining occasions. These efforts helped attract new guests and bring loyalty members back. Second, we continue to make Haidilao distinctive in each market. We stepped up local menu development and refined our menus, building on ingredients and dishes familiar to local guests. We tracked whether new dishes could sustain sales and generate repeat orders after launch. In Singapore, we introduced laksa hot pot and tender pork belly rolls, bringing familiar local flavors to hot pot.

In Korea, we focused on beef, specialty broths and snacks, launching thick-cut beef oyster blade, a rich chestnut and chicken broth and mini milk buns. In Vietnam, we introduced specialty beef and mushroom and vegetable platters to add more choices for local celebrations and group meals. Japan, Canada and Australia also kept adjusting their menus based on seasonal demand, ingredient quality and local taste. We track what guests order, which dishes they order again and how much revenue those dishes contribute. We use that data along with local supply conditions to adjust the menu mix. Our aim is to offer guests more choice while managing menus and running food operations more efficiently.

Third, we continue to strengthen our shared support functions at headquarters. We built on our routine performance tracking by looking at more data together that included table turnover, operating data, member behavior, menu mix, marketing campaigns, costs and expenses. This helps regional teams pinpoint issues and take actions. On the menu side, we use dish click-through rate, repeat orders, sales contribution and gross margin to guide menu changes and new item launches. In marketing, we review the returns on set menus and campaigns and assess their impact on traffic, sales and profit. Restaurants can then adjust pricing and promotions more quickly. At the end of September, Haidilao had more than 10 million registered loyalty members overseas.

As the membership grows, we are focusing on keeping members active and turning that engagement into repeat spending. We look at how often different groups dine with us and how long they go between visits, so restaurants can tailor their outreach. We also share lessons across markets and translate our analysis into practical steps for restaurants. This helps headquarters provide more effective support to frontline teams. Fourth, we continue to expand the Haidilao network at a measured pace with close attention to how new restaurants operate. We opened 3 Haidilao restaurants this quarter, bringing the overseas total to 132 at the end of September. One more has already opened in the fourth quarter and 6 others are preparing to open.

Based on our current progress, we expect 13 openings for the full year. Local teams continue to identify opportunities based on market demand, changes in trade areas, the talent pipeline and projected investment returns. Headquarters supports them by visiting proposed sites, assessing management candidates, reviewing project risks and testing the assumptions behind projections. This helps us pace our openings. Fifth, we continue to advance the Pomegranate Plan and test different restaurant formats across markets. At quarter end of this quarter, we operated 26 restaurants overseas under other brands. They included Malatang, Barbecue, Izakaya and Halal Hot Pot. Several concepts have begun to establish their operating models and show early signs of profitability.

At Hi Bowl, our Malatang concept, we've developed a quick-service model with relatively high seat turnover and relatively low upfront investment. Our Canadian location has been profitable at the restaurant level for several consecutive months, and our Japanese location was profitable at the restaurant level throughout the quarter. Our Izakaya in Japan has also been profitable at the restaurant level for several consecutive months after we refined the menu mix and staffing. Performance still varies considerably across these concepts. The Pomegranate Plan as a whole is still in the investment and business model validation stage. For concepts that are performing well, we'll continue to refine the menu, supply chain and management model.

Where results are below expectations, we'll keep making adjustments and carefully assess the next steps. Overall, we continued to improve existing restaurant operations this quarter while expanding our network and diversifying our business. As conditions evolve across markets, we'll keep our focus on both employees and guests. We'll strengthen the support headquarters provides, improve operations at each restaurant and keep the company on a steady path for long-term growth. Thank you. That concludes my review of third quarter operations. I'll now turn the call over to Lu Li to discuss our financial results.

Lu Li: Thank you, Yu. Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining the call. I am Lu Li, the company's CFO. I'll walk you through Super Hi International's financial and operating results for the third quarter of 2026. Total revenue was $229 million, up 7.1% from $214 million a year ago and up 4.8% from the second quarter. Haidilao restaurant revenue was $206 million, up 2.4% year-over-year. We had a net increase of 6 Haidilao restaurants from a year ago. Overall table turnover and guest visits were also higher, which supported restaurant revenue. Beyond dine-in, we continue to invest in delivery and broaden the range of items available online. Delivery revenue was approximately $7.85 million, up approximately 77.3% year-over-year.

Other revenue was approximately $15.9 million, up 78.7% year-over-year. It came mainly from sales of food products and seasonings from the Haidilao brand and our own central kitchens as well as restaurant revenue from new brands under the Pomegranate Plan. Turning to costs and expenses. Raw materials and consumables cost $79.611 million. Overall gross margin was 65.3%, down 1.4 percentage points year-over-year. Staff costs were $78.791 million or about 34.2% of revenue. That was up about 1 percentage point from 33.2% a year ago. Since the start of the year, we've continued to improve existing restaurant operations while steadily expanding Haidilao and our other brands. We began preparing new locations and putting staff in place ahead of openings.

Preopening investment was higher than a year ago. We also strengthened the shared support functions at headquarters and stepped up investment in building and training our talent pipeline. At Haidilao restaurants, margins remained stable to slightly higher year-over-year. Part of the change in group-level costs reflects our continued investment in expansion and in strengthening those shared management capabilities. Rent and related expenses were $6.483 million or about 2.8% of revenue. Utilities were $8.284 million or about 3.6% of revenue. Both ratios were broadly flat year-over-year. Depreciation and amortization came to $22.384 million or about 9.8% of revenue, down 0.2 percentage points. Travel and other operating expenses were $28.987 million or about 10.9% of revenue, down about 0.2 percentage points.

Those last 2 ratios fell mainly because revenue increased. Operating profit was approximately $9.933 million, with an operating margin of 4.3%. Operating profit fell 21.4% year-over-year, and operating margin declined 1.6 percentage points. This mainly reflected the increased investment I mentioned in business expansion and management capabilities. Compared with the second quarter, operating profit rose by about 22.2% and operating margin increased by 0.6 percentage points from 3.7% to 4.3%. Profit after tax for this quarter was $9.226 million, up 155.6% from $3.593 million a year ago. We recorded a net foreign exchange gain of $4.63 million compared with a net foreign exchange loss of $5.813 million a year earlier. That was a positive swing of approximately $10.443 million.

This year-over-year increase in net profit was, therefore, driven mainly by the improvement in nonoperating foreign exchange results. Net cash generated from operating activities was $36.18 million, up 6.2% from $38.14 million a year ago. At September 30, 2026, bank balances and cash stood at approximately $243 million. Our liquidity remains strong. Let me now turn to our key restaurant metrics. At quarter end, we operated 132 Haidilao restaurants overseas. We recorded about 8.4 million guest visits this quarter, up about 3.7% year-over-year. Average table turnover was 4x per day, up 0.1 turn. Average spending per guest was $24.5, down approximately $0.1.

That mainly reflected a shift in the guest mix with markets where guests spend less per visit accounting for a higher share of our traffic. Average daily revenue per restaurant was $17,700, down about 1.7% year-over-year. Same-store table turnover was 4x per day, up 0.1 turn. While turnover improved overall, changes in average spending per guest and traffic across regions continue to affect same-store sales. Group-wide same-store sales fell 2.3% year-over-year. Southeast Asia was broadly flat. East Asia grew, and same-store sales in North America and other regions remained under pressure. Let me now take a closer look at the figures by region. Performance varied considerably by region this quarter, with Southeast Asia and East Asia remaining broadly resilient.

We opened 2 Haidilao restaurants in Southeast Asia, 1 in Vietnam and 1 in Indonesia. Average table turnover rose from 3.7x to 4x per day year-over-year. Same-store turnover rose by 0.1 turn to 3.9x per day. Overall guest traffic improved. Average spending per guest was $18.7, down $0.4. At same stores, it was slightly higher at $19.2, down $0.1. The differences mainly reflect where the new restaurants opened. Higher table turnover helped lift average daily sales per restaurant by 0.6% to $15,600. Now in East Asia, average table turnover held at 4.9x per day. Same-store turnover was 5x per day, up 0.1 turn. Mature restaurants continue to perform well.

Average spending per guest was $28.8, both overall and at same stores, down slightly year-over-year. This mainly reflected a weaker Japanese yen against the U.S. dollar. At constant exchange rates, overall spending per guest rose $0.40. Average daily sales per restaurant were $20,300, broadly flat year-over-year. We still see room for improvement in North America and other regions. As local dining habits and market conditions evolve, guests in some markets are paying closer attention to price and the dining experience. In some markets, the guest mix and what people want are also changing. That makes it more demanding for restaurants to attract new guests and retain existing ones. We opened 1 new Haidilao restaurant in the United States this quarter.

In North America, both overall and same-store table turnover were 3.4x per day, down 0.6 and 0.5 turns respectively year-over-year. Average spending per guest was $41.5 overall and $40.8 at same stores, both were higher than a year ago. Since the start of the year, we've upgraded what's included in some of our North America set menus with slightly higher starting prices. Average daily sales per restaurant were $19,600, down about 11.3% year-over-year. Canada was the main drag on operating efficiency in the region. Our Canadian team continues to adjust pricing on individual dishes and set menus in line with local dining habits and price sensitivity. It is also offering set menus during off-peak hours to draw guests in.

In other regions, we operate 12 restaurants, all were open for more than 75 days in both the current and prior year quarters and are included in our same-store base. So the metrics are the same for both groups. Average table turnover was 3.5x per day, down 0.2 turn. Average spending per guest was $41.5, up $2.1 year-over-year. At constant exchange rates, it was up $0.20 or broadly flat. Lower turnover weighed on restaurant operating efficiency. Average daily sales per restaurant were $22,300, down about 2.6%. That concludes our review of the company's third quarter 2026 financial and operating results. Thank you. We'll now open the floor to questions from investors and analysts.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The first question comes from Zheshang Securities. [ Ms. Zhong Yichen ], please go ahead.

Unknown Analyst: My name is [ Zhong Yichen]. I actually have 2 questions. The first one is about overseas competition. More and more Chinese restaurant brands now are expanding overseas. The competition has intensified. How does competition vary by country? And what impact has it had on your table turnover and rents? How do you plan to respond as more brands go overseas? That's my first question. My second question is that, since the beginning of the year, Haidilao in China has been building shared support functions and gradually shifting some functional responsibilities away from restaurant managers. How far along are you overseas? Where do restaurant managers and regional teams still have discretion?

Yu Li: Thank you, [ Ms. Zhong ], for your questions. Let me take both of your questions. Now regarding your first question, yes, indeed, more and more Chinese restaurant brands are right now entering the overseas market in recent years. That brings more competition, but it also helps familiarize consumers overseas with Chinese food and expands the market. In some Asia Pacific markets, demand for Chinese food is already well established and competition is more about how restaurants differentiate their menus and guest experience. In Europe and North America, there is still considerable room to build brands. We compete with Chinese restaurants and also a wide range of local operators as well.

The impact on table turnover and rents varies by market. Turnover depends on consumer demands, traffic in the trade area and how well the restaurant is run, among other factors. Competition is one of those factors. When choosing new locations, we look at competition in the trade area, lease terms and also the return we need from the projects. We keep investment costs under tight control. We will keep focusing on both employees and guests. We'll develop more products for local tastes, improve our service experience and strengthen our loyalty program to reach more mainstream local diners. We believe lasting competitiveness comes down to the food, service and our ability to run individual restaurants well and consistently.

Now regarding your second question, we are moving in the same direction as Haidilao in China. We want restaurant managers to spend more time on guests, staff and day-to-day operations. Shared tools and specialist support are gradually being centralized. Headquarters already provides shared support to regional teams in areas including digital systems, operating analysis, financial management and supply chain management. Dining habits, labor laws -- I mean, rules and supply conditions vary considerably from country to country. So we'll continue to give regional teams substantial operating autonomy and flexibility. Regions and restaurants can adapt product development, pricing, marketing, customer acquisition and staff management to local conditions. We maintain common standards for food safety, service quality and compliance.

Shared support gives restaurant managers more time to focus on guests and employees while preserving frontline discretion and improving the quality and efficiency of restaurant operations. That's all for my answer.

Operator: The next question comes from Shengwei Lai with CICC.

Shengwei Lai: I am Shengwei Lai from CICC. I have 3 small questions. The first one is about North America. Well, what are your priorities for improving the North America business over the next few quarters? Which steps are most likely to make a meaningful difference in reaching mainstream local diners, driving repeat visits and improving your restaurant footprint? What do you expect to see? And when do you expect to see the results? My second question is about the restaurant growth outlook. Since the fourth quarter began, what changes have you seen in consumer demand and restaurant traffic in Southeast Asia, East Asia and North America? Looking ahead to next year, what will drive same-store growth by region?

And which markets are you most confident about? And my last question is about margin. Now we actually see that you have put in new investment this quarter. What will be the main levers for improving the group's operating margin next year? How much room is there to improve labor productivity, source locally and turn around underperforming restaurants? How will you pace investment in shared profit -- I mean, shared support functions as revenue grows?

Yu Li: All right. This is Yu Li. I'm going to take your first question. Now regarding North America, North America has been affected by changes in demand and competition locally. We also have work to do on understanding the market, managing operations and responding more quickly. We were slow to spot and act on some market changes. We've begun restructuring the management team to strengthen local operations and help our teams pick up on changes sooner and execute faster. We're working on 3 fronts. First, we are reviewing and adjusting our local operating strategy to give guests more reasons to visit.

Some restaurants have changed dishes and set menus based on market feedback, launched themed weekend events and focused more on students. We'll keep tracking what works and adjust our approach to each market and restaurant. Second, we are managing each restaurant more closely and refining the network. We'll take a closer look at traffic by location and time of the day, menu mix, staffing and operating costs. This will help us target improvements at individual restaurants. Third, we want to broaden our guest base. While retaining existing diners, we will reach out to more mainstream local guests with targeted products, campaigns and local marketing. We want to attract more new diners and gradually bring more of them back.

We hope to see early results from some marketing and operational changes over the next 1 to 2 quarters. It will take longer to assess shifts in the guest mix, where repeat visit rates settle and whether individual restaurants sustain their improvement. That's my answer for your first question. Now Ms. Lu Li is going to take the other 2 of your questions.

Lu Li: Now regarding your second question, basically, overseas markets are moving into the traditional peak dining season. Demand for holiday and year-end group meals has increased. Traffic has improved overall, and table turnover is higher year-over-year. Some markets in East and Southeast Asia stood out, and East Asia as a whole held steady. Some North American restaurants remain under pressure. We're also seeing encouraging signs in demand for business gatherings and company dinners. Our overseas restaurants are preparing to accommodate these groups and capture peak season demand. Looking ahead to 2027, we're confident that Southeast Asia and East Asia can maintain steady operations.

Same-store growth will continue to come mainly from locally developed products, the loyalty program, repeat visits and closer management at the restaurant level. In North America, we'll focus on improving existing restaurants, reaching more mainstream local diners, refining our menu and pricing and getting more guests to act on our campaigns. Overall, our priority remains running each restaurant well. We'll make the most of the peak season and keep improving the guest experience and operating efficiency to support future same-store growth. Now regarding your last question, which is about our operating efficiency. There's room to improve profitability at existing restaurants. We make decisions with operating quality in mind and balance near-term performance with long-term development.

At existing restaurants, we'll improve staffing and scheduling, strengthen procurement and source more locally. For restaurants that are falling short of expectations, we'll make targeted improvements or adjust the network. The aim is to improve efficiency and profitability at individual restaurants. Across the group, preparations for new Haidilao restaurants, new concepts under the Pomegranate Plan and shared support capabilities at headquarters all require upfront resources and investment that can affect group margins in the short term. We'll pace investment according to how the businesses evolve and what stage they're at and keep reviewing the returns on that spending. Overall, we're confident that we can keep improving profitability at existing restaurants.

We will continue making the long-term investments we need and balance them with near-term operating performance to support steady, sustainable growth. Thank you.

Operator: The next question comes from Huatai Securities. Jun Zeng, please go ahead.

Jun Zeng: I also have 3 small questions. The first one is, how did average spending per guest change year-over-year by region at constant exchange rates? How is price sensitivity changing across markets? Have you added low-price set menus or smaller portions? And how has that affected spending per guest and table turnover? With exchange rates still volatile, how do you quantify the point at which the trade-off between spending per guest and table turnover makes sense? The second question is about new restaurant openings. Now operations and profitability in East and Southeast Asia have been fairly stable across the market following recent adjustments. Are you considering taking what has worked in Asia into new markets?

How do you weigh adding more restaurants in existing countries against expanding into new regions? My third question is about delivery. Delivery revenue is growing quickly. Can every restaurant offer delivery? Are you targeting a share of revenue from delivery that protects the dine-in experience? How does average spending on delivery compare with dine-in? And what are the respective gross margins?

Yu Li: Thank you, Mr. Zeng, for your questions. First of all, regarding your first question, in the third quarter, at constant exchange rates, average spending per guest in Southeast Asia fell about $0.50 year-over-year. That mainly reflected where we opened our new restaurants. Most of this year's openings in the region were in Indonesia and Vietnam, where spending per guest is relatively lower. In East Asia, spending per guest rose by $0.40 at constant exchange rates. In North America, it rose by $2.6 year-over-year, mainly because we've refined, upgraded and introduced menu items since the first half of the year and adjusted some set menus.

In other regions, spending per guest rose by $0.20 at constant exchange rates, reflecting a small impact from menu changes. We believe that price sensitivity varies across markets, so pricing needs to vary too. In North America, the third quarter numbers show a clear impact on table turnover from changes in spending per guest. Market conditions and guest needs can change very quickly. We also realize that regional managers need to be closely involved in local operations so they can improve the experience while offering good value. When we weigh spending per guest against table turnover, we look at each restaurant's overall performance.

Headquarters look at table turnover alongside the menu mix, returns on marketing spend and gross margins to help restaurants adjust pricing and promotions. So that was my answer for your first question. Regarding your second question, yes, we have operated in Southeast and East Asia for years and have built up considerable experience adapting to local markets. Third quarter average table turnover in Southeast Asia rose from 3.7x to 4x per day year-over-year. East Asia held at 4.9x. Overall operating metrics remain fairly resilient in both regions. What travels across markets is our expertise in site selection, talent development, supply chain management, menu development and restaurant operations.

But the menu mix, pricing and marketing still need to reflect local demand in each country. We'll look at both adding restaurants in existing markets and entering new areas where we already have brand awareness, a supply chain and trained staff, and a denser network can improve operating efficiency. We'll also weigh coverage across trade areas, traffic at existing locations and whether a new restaurant could draw traffic away from them. For new regions and countries, we'll take a closer look at demand, spending power, competition, supply conditions and the availability of management talent. We've done some initial work in markets and some markets in Europe and South America, but it's still early, and there's a lot to do.

Site visits and deeper research will help us understand local conditions and prepare before we move ahead gradually. Our approach is still to identify opportunities from the ground up, with restaurant-level operating quality and long-term investment returns determining the pace of opening new stores. So that was my answer for your second question. The last question was about delivery. Now delivery has been one of our fastest-growing businesses over the past few quarters. In the third quarter of 2026, delivery revenue reached approximately $7.85 million, up 77.3% year-over-year and representing about 3.4% of group revenue. Delivery growth has come mainly from new products, marketing, broader distinction -- sorry, broader distribution and closer partnerships with local delivery platforms.

Delivery serves different occasions and operates very differently from dine-in. The delivery menu mainly offers simple meals and single-person sets. On average, a meal for one costs less on delivery than when dining in, and gross margin is also slightly lower. Delivery has lower labor costs, but it also incurs extra costs such as platform commissions. That results in different cost and profit structures. Haidilao's core strengths are food, service and the in-restaurant experience. We'll protect the experience as we grow our delivery business. At each location, we consider kitchen capacity, staffing, how busy dine-in is and local delivery demand before deciding what to offer on which platform and how. Almost all Haidilao restaurants now offer delivery services.

We look at whether delivery generates incremental revenue and profit and makes a meaningful contribution. We don't set a fixed target for its share of revenue. That's all. Thank you.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The next question comes from [ Wei Jiabao ] with CITIC Securities.

Unknown Analyst: I am [ Wei Jiabao ] with CITIC Securities. I have 2 questions. The first one is about Hi Bowl and other brands. Now Hi Bowl has expanded into markets including Singapore and Australia, and Haidilao's Dai Pai Dong concept is planned for Vietnam. Could you update us on the Pomegranate Plan, including priority brands, opening targets, markets for expansion and operating models at representative locations? And my second question is about your plan for dividends and share buybacks.

Lu Li: Thank you for the questions. Now regarding the Pomegranate Plan, the plan builds on years of experience in overseas restaurant operations, supply chains and talent management. The aim of it is to develop more dining formats suited to local consumers. To date, we have more than 10 brands and more than 30 Pomegranate Plan restaurants overseas. As Mr. Yu Li mentioned earlier, Hi Bowl, our Malatang concept, is among the concepts with a relatively clear and proven operating model. We have locations open in Canada, Japan, Australia and Singapore and projects in preparation in other countries, including the United States and United Kingdom.

Now we also see strong operating and expansion potential in hot pot, our Halal Hot Pot brand in Indonesia and our Izakaya in Japan. We've also brought in Xiangxiang Hunan Cuisine and are exploring a new model through a joint venture with an established Chinese restaurant brand. In October, we opened 1 restaurant each in South Korea, Vietnam and Indonesia. By combining the partners' strengths, we hope to use Super Hi's existing overseas platform to make it easier for new brands to enter overseas markets. Now on the Haidilao Dai Pai Dong concept you mentioned, we are preparing the first location in Vietnam and expect it to open by year-end.

At the current stage, we will first validate the restaurant-level economics of each format before deciding which concept can expand rapidly. We look at guest acceptance, revenue mix, gross profit -- I mean gross margin, labor productivity and investment returns. Where concepts perform well, we will continue to build the capabilities they need. Where results fall short, we'll make timely adjustments. Now regarding the second question of yours about dividends and share buybacks. We generated approximately $36.18 million in net cash from operating activities in the third quarter. At the end of September, bank balances and cash were approximately $243 million. Overall, liquidity remains strong.

In allocating capital, we will consider the funding needs of existing operations and planned investment in new Haidilao restaurants. We will carefully evaluate dividends and share repurchases in light of cash flow, CapEx plans, our overall financial position and shareholders' interests and follow the Board's decision-making procedures. Thank you.

Operator: Now the next question comes from [ Li Zhenni ] with Founder Securities.

Unknown Analyst: I have 2 questions here. The first question is, how are this year's new restaurants doing in terms of operating performance and margins? What investment payback periods are you seeing? My second question is, how many overseas loyalty members do you have? What shares of revenue do they account for? How are member acquisition, repeat visits and engagement trending? What are you doing differently with member behavior data and digital tools? These are my 2 questions.

Yu Li: Thank you, [ Ms. Li ], for your questions. Now about new store performance. Over the past few years, we've strengthened our upfront investment reviews and preopening preparations. That includes refining site selection criteria, restaurant design and staffing pipeline requirements. New restaurants are ramping up faster overall. By the end of September 2026, 6 new restaurants had opened, 5 generated positive cash flow in their first month, and those restaurants averaged more than 4 table turns per day in October. We continue to assess new projects against payback requirements of roughly 3 to 5 years, depending on the region. Most new restaurants currently have expected payback periods within plan.

We'll continue improving how we evaluate and prepare new restaurants and raise operating efficiency and restaurant-level profitability to support steady network growth. Now your second question is about our overseas loyalty members. Our loyalty program is an important part of strengthening how we engage with guests. At the end of September 2026, Haidilao had more than 10 million registered members overseas. Member spending accounted for approximately 90% of Haidilao restaurant revenue. As the program grows, we are refining the benefits at each membership tier. To keep members active, we offer exclusive discounts on dishes, run campaigns to bring back inactive members and provide birthday and tier rewards.

We've also launched the Haidilao App in several overseas markets, added more rewards to the points store and introduced tiered point redemption. These steps improve member experience and encourage repeat visits and stronger loyalty. On the digital side, we are deepening our analysis of member spending habits, including visit frequency, time between visits and menu preferences. We combine member, menu and operating data so restaurants can make better decisions on campaigns, guest retention and menu promotions to improve operating performance. That's my answer for your 2 questions. Thank you.

Operator: All right. Thank you for the questions. Now this concludes our earnings call. Thank you, investors and analysts, for your participation. I'll see you next time. [Statements in English on this transcript were spoken by an interpreter present on the live call.]

#2961. Steelers suddenly have a major mess

Last night, Steelers fans who weren't already familiar with the name "Burt Lauten" became instantly acquainted with him, when his name appeared in large, bold print as the person announcing the benching of quarterback Aaron Rodgers. And Lauten will be earning every bit of pay and then some in the coming hours.

Lauten serves as the team's senior director of communications. He's basically in charge of P.R. And the Steelers have a P.R. mess unlike any they've ever experienced.

The benching of Rodgers has prompted a predictable reaction. Rodgers went straight to the McAfee show and pressed "play" on his various complaints and concerns about coach Mike McCarthy.

It was specific. It was detailed. It was damning. The things Rodgers said created the clear impression that McCarthy should not be coaching the team.

This becomes a problem that goes beyond P.R. strategy. Owner Art Rooney II needs to get involved, determine whether Rodgers's version is accurate, and take action.

It's simple. If what Rodgers is saying is remotely true, he should not currently be the coach of the team. If Rodgers isn't telling the truth, the Steelers need to set the record straight immediately.

However it goes, it's a mess. A gigantic mess. An unprecedented mess for the Steelers and perhaps for any NFL franchise.
